kept_transcript: Right now you are moving. If you are in Britain the ground under you is carrying you east at about a thousand kilometers an hour. At the equator it is faster than a jet airliner and you feel nothing at all. So what would happen if earth stops spinning? Not slowly all at once. Now imagine the impossible. Earth's rock stops turning in an instant but the air does not. Nothing has told it to stop. At the equator the atmosphere would keep going east at more than one and a half thousand kilometers an hour. That is faster than the speed of sound and several times faster than the strongest gust of wind ever measured. The oceans would keep moving too and rise up against every eastern coast. Why east? Because that is the way we were all already going. Anything not fixed to the ground would carry on east as well just as you lurch forwards when a bus breaks hard. Here in Britain the wind would arrive at about a thousand kilometers an hour. But here is a strange detail. Stand exactly at the north pole and you would hardly notice. You were barely moving in the first place. You were just turning on the spot once a day. And it cannot happen. There is no break. The energy stored in earth's spin is as much as all the sunlight that reaches earth in about 40 ,000 years. Nothing in our solar system could take that away in a moment. Why don't you feel it? Because the speed is steady. Sit in a smooth airliner and you can pour a drink without spilling a drop. Nothing pushes you because nothing is changing. Your body only notices a change in speed. Never the speed itself. You can still see the spin. Every single day the sun does not rise. Your side of earth turns towards it. Earth turns from west to east. And that is why the sun always comes up in the east and why the stars wheel across the sky at night. The spin does leave clues. Because the ground at the equator swings round so fast you weigh about half of 1 % less there than at the poles. And the whole planet bulges. Earth is about 43 kilometers wider across the equator than it is from pole to pole. In 1851 in Paris, Leon Foucault hung a heavy ball from a wire 67 meters long and set it swinging. Over the hours the line of its swing slowly turned. The pendulum was not turning. The floor was. Anyone could stand there and watch earth spin without looking at the sky. So a sudden stop is a thought experiment. What about a slow one? Suppose earth slowed down gently over thousands of years until it did not turn at all. Remember that bulge at the equator? The spin is what holds the oceans out there. Without it the water would drain away towards the poles. Map makers have modeled it. The seas gather into two great polar oceans and a single enormous band of dry land wraps around the middle of the world. And the day itself would change. With no spin at all, the sun would cross the sky just once as earth went round it. One day would last a whole year. Six months of daylight then six months of night. The day side would bake under a sun that never sets and the night side would freeze in the dark with the wind always pouring from one side to the other. We have a neighbor that comes close. Venus turns once every 243 earth days. And it turns backwards. Its day is longer than its year. If you saw our Venus film you know how strange that world became. Here is the twist. Earth is slowing down already right now. The moon pulls on our oceans and raises the tides. As earth turns beneath those tides the water drags a little against the seabed like a hand resting on a spinning wheel. Every day a tiny amount of spin is lost. Where does it go? Into the moon. The tides tug the moon forwards and it drifts about four centimeters further from us every year. If you saw our moon film this is the other half of that story. And the moon shows us where this road leads. Long ago earth's pull slowed the moon's own spin until one turn took exactly one orbit. That is why the moon always shows us the same face. It did not stop spinning. It got locked. How do we know? Ancient eclipses. Astronomers in Babylon, China and Medieval Europe wrote down where and when the sun went dark. If earth had kept spinning at today's rate those eclipses would have been seen from places hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. The records only fit if the day has been growing longer by nearly two thousandths of a second every century. That sounds like nothing but give it time. Corals lay down a fine growth line every day and a thicker band each year. Fossil corals about 380 million years old show about 400 daily lines in a year. Back then a day was only about 22 hours long. So who notices two thousandths of a second? Your phone does. Since the late 1960s the second has been set by atomic clocks which do not care how fast earth turns but the day measured by the sun does not quite fit the clocks. So since 1972 timekeepers have added an extra second to the world's clocks 27 times to keep noon where it belongs. The last one came at the end of 2016 and the day wobbles. Earth's molten core, its oceans and even melting ice all nudged the spin. In the last few years the planet has actually been running a touch fast and some days have come in more than a millisecond short. Timekeepers now plan to stop adding leap seconds by 2035. So earth will never stop spinning even the moon's slow break would need tens of billions of years to lock our day to its month and long before then the sun would have changed beyond recognition. Your days will stay 24 hours to within a blink. What if the most surprising thing about your day is not that it might end but that it has always been changing? The bigger question is the one underneath all of this. Something set earth spinning in the first place about four and a half billion years ago. Every sunrise you have ever seen is that first push still running down.

kept_transcript: A robot built to last 90 days on Mars kept going for more than 14 years. Why did it survive so long and what finally stopped it? Mars does not crush machines, it does not melt them, it wears them down slowly in ways you already know from home. The cold that kills a phone battery, the dust on a windscreen, a tire that finally splits. So could a robot survive on Mars? At first glance, Mars looks like a desert you could drive across. Red rock, rolling dunes, a hazy sky. It is a trick of the eye. The air is so thin that the pressure at the ground is less than 1 % of Earth's. The average temperature is about minus 60 degrees. At the first Viking landing site, nights fell to nearly minus 90. And because the air is thin and Mars has no global magnetic shield, radiation reaches the ground. Curiosity measured it. In one day on Mars, the dose is roughly what you would get in three months on Earth. A person would need a pressure suit just to stand there. But a robot does not breathe, and it does not get sick. So the thin air and the radiation are not what usually ends a robot's life on Mars. The killers are quieter. Cold. Dust. Wear. Of the robots that landed safely and went to work, most were stopped by one of those three. And whatever goes wrong, nobody can rush to help. A radio signal takes from about three minutes to more than 20 to cross between the planets, each way. Nobody can steer a rover live like a toy car. Every robot on Mars has to look after itself between messages from home. Start with the cold, because you have felt what it does. Take your phone out on a freezing day and watch the battery drop. Electronics and batteries hate deep cold. On Mars, every night is colder than any winter night in a British garden, so a rover spends part of its power just keeping its own insides warm, like a person burning energy to shiver. That only works while power keeps coming in. In 2009, the rover Spirit drove into soft sand at a place the team called Troy and its wheels sank. It could not climb out. It could not tilt its solar panels towards the low winter sun. As the days shortened, its power fell. On the 22nd of March 2010, Spirit sent its last message. Spirit did not break apart. It got stuck, and winter did the rest. Its mission had been planned for 90 days. It worked for more than six years. The cold can be even more direct. In 2008, the Phoenix lander touched down near the North Pole of Mars to dig for ice. When winter came, it went silent. Two years later, a spacecraft in orbit photographed it again. Its solar panels looked broken, most likely bent by the weight of frost and ice that had built up over the winter. Spirit had a twin on the far side of Mars. It lasted much longer, and the reason was the wind. Mars is a dusty world. Fine red dust settles on everything, including solar panels. A panel under dust is like a windscreen nobody wipes. Less and less light gets through. A rover that runs on sunlight slowly starves. Opportunity should have starved within months. Instead, again and again, Martian wind and passing dust devils swept its panels clean. The team called them cleaning events. Each one gave the rover back its power, and it kept driving. 90 days became years. Years became more than 14. Then in 2018, a storm grew until it wrapped the whole planet. The sky over Opportunity grew so dark that almost no sunlight reached its panels. On the 10th of June 2018, Opportunity sent its last signal. Engineers on Earth sent more than a thousand commands over the next eight months, asking it to wake up. It never answered. What finally stopped the most successful rover of its time was not cold or rock. It was the sky turning off. Why does dust matter so much? Because on Mars, there is no rain to wash anything clean. The land at InSight spent four years listening for Marsquakes and felt more than a thousand of them, but dust kept building on its panels. In December 2022, it went quiet the same way, not broken, just out of light. Even a robot that never runs out of power wears out. Curiosity runs on a nuclear power source, a small supply of plutonium that gives off heat day and night, dust or no dust. When the 2018 storm darkened Opportunity's sky, Curiosity kept working in another part of the planet, but its wheels had a different problem. They are thin aluminum, made light enough to fly to Mars. In 2013, the team noticed holes. Sharp rocks were punching through like a tire on broken glass. Since then, the drivers have planned routes around the sharpest ground, and they photograph the wheels to watch the damage grow. Why not just build the wheels tougher? Because every kilogram has to be launched off Earth, carried for months, slowed from thousands of kilometers an hour, and set down gently on another world. On Mars, strength always has to be weighed against getting there at all. And then there is the little helicopter. Ingenuity was built for up to five test flights over 30 days, in air 1 % as thick as ours. It flew 72 times over almost three years. In January 2024, after its last landing, images showed damage to its rotor blades. It could not fly again. It is still standing on Mars. So, could a robot survive on Mars? Yes, not forever, and not alone. The robots that last are the ones with a steady supply of power, heaters to fight the night, and a team on Earth who drive carefully around every sharp rock. Sometimes they also need luck, in the shape of a gust of wind at the right moment. That is what Mars teaches. Survival there is not one heroic moment. It is a thousand small decisions, made from another planet every single day. Power that does not depend on a clear sky, a way to stay warm through the night, a shell tough enough for sharp ground, and someone at home watching. What if the real story of every Mars robot is not how it died, but how long people kept it going? The bigger question sits in the tracks they leave. Every robot that stops on Mars stays exactly where it stopped, and the dust slowly covers it.

kept_transcript: Right now, the invisible magnetic shield around our planet is weakening and the North Magnetic Pole is racing across the Arctic towards Siberia. One day, North and South will swap places. Will life on Earth survive that danger? Or will our air blow away into space? No. We will survive. Life has lived through hundreds of magnetic flips, so why do satellites in orbit already have to shut down over the South Atlantic? 1905 – Central France A physicist, named Bernard Brunez, is chipping rock from a hillside near the village of Pont -Forain. He is looking at ancient lava that poured over wet clay long ago, baking the mud underneath into red brick. As lava or brick cools, tiny grains of iron oxide inside it lock into line with Earth's magnetic field, like microscopic compass needles freezing in place. Brunez takes samples back to his lab. He expects them to point north, like the compass on his desk. Instead, the lava and the baked clay both point almost exactly the opposite way. At first, scientists wonder if the rock played a chemical trick on itself. Why would a hillside point the wrong way? 23 years later, in 1929, Japanese geophysicist Motonori Matuyama tests volcanic rocks across Japan and Manchuria. The younger rocks point north. The older ones, from early in the ice age, point south. Today, we date that last switch to about 780 ,000 years ago. The whole planet had turned its magnetic field upside down. If the poles flipped then, what secret engine builds a magnet the size of a world? And why does it ever lose its way? About 3 ,000 kilometers beneath your shoes lies the engine that runs every compass on Earth. Down there, the outer core is a churning ocean of iron -rich liquid metal, about as hot as the surface of the sun. Because Earth spins and heat rises from the center, that liquid metal twists into giant, spiraling currents. Moving metal carries electric currents, and those currents generate our magnetic field. Most of the time, Earth spin keeps those iron currents lined up, giving us one steady north pole and one steady south pole. However, a liquid ocean is messy. Swirling eddies form in the molten iron and fight the main flow. What if enough backwards eddies grow strong together? Then the main field weakens, wobbles, and tips all the way over. Where new rock spreads across the ocean floor, it records every flip like a barcode on a packet. Over the last 83 million years, Earth has flipped 183 times. And since German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss began measuring the field strength in the 1830s, it has dropped by about 9%. Why is it dropping now, and where on Earth is our shield already sagging inward today? High above South America and the South Atlantic Ocean, the magnetic shield has developed a deep dent. Since 2013, three European spacecraft called Swarm have mapped this weak spot, the South Atlantic Anomaly. Above most of the planet, our field holds trapped space radiation safely out beyond 600 kilometers. Over the South Atlantic, because a patch of magnetic field on the liquid core has already flipped backwards, the shield sags down to 200 kilometers, half the height of the space station. On the ground, you feel nothing. The air above you stops those particles long before they reach you. Up in low Earth orbit, it is another story. The Hubble Space Telescope flies through that dent on seven to nine orbits in a row every day, and each time it stops observing, because stray radiation would swamp its instruments. Instruments on the outside of the space station take the extra radiation too, and satellite operators often shut down anything non -essential as they cross. Since 1970, that weak spot has widened and split into two lobes. A weaker global field, a racing pole, a growing dent over the Atlantic. Case closed? Are we overdue for a total flip right now? Wrong. We are not overdue, and today's drop is probably just a normal breath in a restless planet. Magnetic records in ancient rock and sediment show that today's field is about as strong as it has been for 100 ,000 years and twice its average over the last million. Better still, the field often dips without flipping at all. About 41 ,000 years ago, during the Lachamp event, the shield tried to flip, dropped nearly to zero, and snapped back. How did scientists unlock that mystery year by year? In northern New Zealand, giant cowrie trees grew right through it, and their trunks were dug out of swamp mud intact. As the shield dropped to about 6 % of today's strength, more cosmic rays hit the upper air, creating a spike of radioactive carbon that every tree ring recorded like a diary. The collapse took a few hundred years, and the weak phase lasted less than a thousand years. Modern humans were already arriving in Europe, and people from Europe to Southeast Asia were painting caves and looking up at the night sky. Why didn't the solar wind strip away their air and turn Earth into a second Mars? That is the scariest idea people repeat about a magnetic flip. What if the solar wind blew Earth's atmosphere into space? Let us test that fear with numbers. First, Earth's magnetic field never vanishes completely. The main north -south magnet may weaken to about a tenth of its normal strength, while smaller, temporary poles pop up around it. Second, we have a shield that never switches off, the air itself. The nitrogen and oxygen above your head weigh about a kilogram on every square centimeter, as much as a layer of water 10 meters deep covering the planet. Even if the magnetic field dropped to zero tomorrow, almost all fast particles from space would slam into gas molecules high in the air and stop long before reaching the ground. Why did Mars lose its air? Because Mars is small, with just over a third of Earth's gravity, and that loss took billions of years. A flip on Earth takes only a few thousand years, far too brief to steal a heavy planet's atmosphere. Across millions of years of fossils, scientists find no link between magnetic reversals and mass extinctions. The real job in a modern flip would be hardening satellites and power grids against solar storms. So what would you actually see if you stood outside in the middle of one? For a few thousand years, Earth would not have two magnetic poles. Models of the liquid core show the field tangling into several poles at once, popping up in unexpected places. You might have a south pole over Africa and a north pole over Tahiti in the middle of the Pacific. A pocket compass would point toward whichever pole stood nearest, while migrating birds, whales, and sea turtles leaned on the sun, the stars, and the coastline as their map redrew itself. And whenever a solar wind gust brushed against those scattered poles, the aurora would not stay locked in the Arctic and Antarctic. Curtains of green and crimson light would funnel down toward the middle of the planet, shimmering above London, Cairo, Mumbai, and Sydney on clear nights. For 40 to 400 human generations, the northern lights would become the lights of the whole world, until the liquid iron deep underfoot settled and locked the compass south. Our shield is not a brittle wall that shatters, it is a living ocean of metal 3 ,000 kilometers down, shifting and painting the sky.

kept_transcript: The cloud deck is already around you. Cream, ochre and rust roll past with no shore in the curve. What would you see if you fall into Jupiter? The mystery starts here, not on a poster. This colored weather is not ground. Nothing solid is waiting to stop you. That is the stake, and it is already true. The journey from here is down through the layers. Cloud, then darker cloud, then a dark where sunlight gives up and still no floor. Look at what your eyes get first. Bands, not continents. Pale zones and darker belts wrap a world that turns in about 10 hours. So the stripes are a fast day written on a deep atmosphere, not a map of land. The great red spot sits in that weather, a storm still wider than Earth, spinning for centuries, winds faster than a hurricane. Color is cloud. Why does it look so finished when you are this close? Because the top deck is thin and it is bright. Sunlight hits ammonia ice crystals and throws cream back at you. A little deeper, other chemicals stain the air rust and brown. You are not seeing Jupiter's body, you are seeing its weather. The mass underneath, about 318 Earths, hides under a few tens of kilometers of scenery. Wind, a horizon made of cloud, no mountain to judge distance by. The mystery is how something this vivid can be so empty of ground. But the picture that brought you here is only the lid. You're probably wondering if it ever stops, it doesn't. Not the way a canyon stops or a sea or Europa's ice. There is no crust under the paint. The line on a diagram that says surface is a pressure, about one bar, the weight of Earth's air at sea level. Useful for measuring height, useless for standing. Step onto that line and you step onto atmosphere. Why call it a fall if there is no bottom to hit? Because down is still real. Gravity does not need a floor. Jupiter's mass gathers you inward and the air thickens as you go. Pressure climbs, temperature climbs. You are not dropping toward rock. You are sinking into a planet that stays atmosphere until the word itself gets tired. What if the stripes were a shell with an ocean under them and a seabed after that? That is the picture a rocky world trained you to expect. Deeper cloud is still cloud. When you reach water, it is not a sea with a coast. It is hotter, heavier weather wrapped all the way around. There is no shoreline in the dark and no moment where falling turns into standing. Now the question changes. What did a machine actually see? On the 7th of December 1995, a probe about the size of a large suitcase went in for us. It hit the atmosphere, slowed under a parachute and sent numbers home from inside the weather. It lasted about 58 minutes. In that hour, it fell roughly 150 kilometers below the deck you can see. Pressure rose to about 22 times Earth's air at sea level. Temperature climbed to about 150 degrees Celsius. Then the signal stopped. The machine was crushed and cooked. It still had not touched ground. Why does that hour matter more than a painting of the clouds? Because it is the only time we have been inside and heard back. 22 bars is already far past a stroll. It is still the porch. The center is tens of thousands of kilometers further in. The probe died before the hall. It went in through a dry hotspot where the water was thinner than models hoped. The unknown is not only the deep interior. One hole is not the whole planet. The floor was still absent and the probe was not a window. The view has to be built from what light does. At first, you would still see. The deck is bright from above and gloomy from below. Cream light leaks through thinner patches, rust walls of clouds slide past. For a short while, the sun is a smear, not a disc, and the bands become a ceiling. Then the ceiling closes. A short fall under the visible deck and the sunlight is already losing. Ammonia clouds, then a dirtier layer, then water clouds, each one another blanket. Photons from the sun scatter, get absorbed, and quit. What would you see once the last pale leak is gone? Not a night sky. There is no sky down there. Merc, then black, and maybe a flash of lightning in the water cloud layer. Juno has watched that lightning from above. From inside, it would be a flash in a room with no walls. Why does the dark arrive before any talk of a core? Because the clouds are thick long before the pressure becomes exotic. Your eyes tap out early. The rest of the journey is real and it is invisible. If you came for a landscape, this is the term. The landscape was the lid. However far the probe got, it died with a very long way still to go. Deeper than sight, the planet changes state. Keep going in your mind, past the black. Pressure keeps climbing toward millions of times the air you breathe. Temperature climbs with it. Hydrogen stops acting like a gas you could wave through. It becomes a fluid. Deeper still, that fluid behaves like a metal, metallic hydrogen, conducting electricity the way a wire does, except there is no wire. There is a planet -sized current. That current is why Jupiter wears a huge magnetic field. You would not see a shining cavern. The honest view is dark amber pressure, slow and hot, with no floor rising to meet you. Surely then, a core, a hard seed in the middle, even if you never reach it. Juno listened to small tugs on its path and the mass inside does not sit like a marble. The heavy elements look smeared through a large, inner region, a dilute core, not a boulder you could stand on, a gradient. The center is still immense, pressure beyond the probe's porch heat on the order of tens of thousands of degrees, and it is still not ground. So the payoff of the fall fits in one breath. You would see the cloud deck, banded and vast, and a storm bigger than Earth if your path finds it. You would see that color thicken, dim and close. You might see one flash of lightning. Then you would see nothing, because the rest of Jupiter is not a sight. It is a weight. The probe's last report was weather, heat and pressure, and then silence, with no surface in the data. What happens next, kept honest, is not an impact. It is a fade into a fluid world that never offers you a place to stop. Zoom out just enough to see the deck again, stripes, a red oval, a bright dot you could cover with a thumb. The mystery is that this peaceful picture is the whole show your eyes were ever going to get. Everything past it is measurement. Why does that change the bright dot? Because planet was doing too much work. Earth lets you stand. Europa, under its ice, at least offers a shell. Jupiter offers a fall with no arrival. The point is not a monster in the clouds. The point is a category error, expecting a flaw from a world that is atmosphere all the way into a metal. Once you know that, the bands stop being decoration. They are the last thing you would see, until a bigger question tags along. Saturn wears stripes too. Uranus and Neptune hide under colder haze. If you fell into any of them, would you ever find a flaw?

kept_transcript: There is a star coming towards us, so how close will it get and should you worry? This is not a guess and not a rumor, the star has been measured and it is heading almost straight at the sun. Its name is Gliese 710. In about 1 .3 million years it will pass closer to us than any star we know of. It will not hit anything, but it will sail right through the outer edge of our solar system. Right now, Gliese 710 is about 62 light years away in the constellation of serpents, the serpent. It is an orange dwarf, a little smaller and cooler than the sun, with about 60 % of the sun's mass. You cannot see it, it is far too faint for your eyes on even the darkest night. You would need binoculars just to find it. So why does it matter? Because of the way it moves. Most stars drift slowly sideways across our sky, year after year. Gliese 710 hardly drifts at all. It is coming towards us at about 14 kilometers every second, more than 50 ,000 kilometers an hour, and almost none of that motion is sideways. When something barely moves across your view but keeps getting closer, it is heading for you, like a car on a long straight road at night. Its headlights do not slide left or right, they just grow. If you saw our film on the nearest star, you met Proxima Centauri, about four light years away. Proxima is our nearest neighbor today. But stars move, and the title of nearest does not last forever. How do we know where it will be in a million years? For a long time we did not. We were not even sure it would come close at all. In the late 1990s a satellite called Hipparcos measured the star's position and motion. The best guess then was that it would pass about a light year from the Sun and the uncertainty was huge. Then came Gaia, the European spacecraft that has measured more than a billion stars. With every new release of its data the path came into sharper focus and the star kept coming closer. The latest Gaia measurements put the closest approach at about a fifth of a light year. That is about 10 to 13 ,000 times further than Earth is from the Sun, five times closer than the old estimate. That still sounds far, so let's shrink it, make the gap between the Sun and Earth one centimeter. Neptune, our outermost planet, is then 30 centimeters away, about the length of a ruler, and Gliese 710 passes more than a hundred meters away, the length of a football pitch. So the star will not come anywhere near the planets, but what is out there a hundred meters from the Sun? Something we have never seen. Far beyond the planets the Sun is wrapped in a vast cloud of ice. Trillions of frozen bodies, the leftovers from when the planets formed, drifting so far out that the Sun's pull on them is barely a whisper. It is called the Oort cloud and it is still one of the great unknowns of our solar system. Nobody has ever seen it directly. We know it is there because of the comets that fall out of it on journeys that take them hundreds of thousands of years or more. Its inner edge is thought to start a few thousand times further out than Earth. Its outer edge may reach a hundred thousand. Sunlight, which gets to us in eight minutes, would take months to reach the place where Gliese 710 will pass and that is exactly where the star is going. Straight through the Oort cloud. A star passing through the cloud is like a hand brushing through a bowl of floating marbles. Its gravity nudges the comets nearest its path, some get flung out into the galaxy, others are knocked onto new orbits that fall in towards the Sun. The calculations suggest that Gliese 710 will send about 10 extra comets a year falling in close enough for us to see and it will keep happening for three to four million years. But here is the strange part. The comets do not arrive while the star is passing. Why? Because they are so far out that falling in takes hundreds of thousands of years. By the time the shower is at its height, Gliese 710 will already be heading away again, shrinking back into the dark. Should anyone worry? Not much. Most comets that fall in never come close to Earth. Jupiter and Saturn throw many of them back out or steer them away. What the people of that far future get is a sky with more comets in it for a very long time. So what would you see? Imagine standing on Earth on the night of the closest pass. A new star has been brightening for thousands of years. Now it is the brightest star in the whole night sky, about three times brighter than Sirius and as bright as Jupiter at its best. And it glows orange. It will not light up the night like the moon and it will not warm anyone, it is still billions of times fainter than our Sun. But it will move. Most stars look fixed for a lifetime. This one will creep across the sky by about the width of the full moon every 35 years. Then, slowly, it will fade and drift away for good. Is this the first time a star has come this close? Not at all. Gliese 710 will not be the first star to pass this way. About 70 ,000 years ago, a dim red pair of stars now called Scholz's star skimmed through the outer Oort cloud less than a light year from the Sun. It was too small and too faint to stir up much. And about 2 .8 million years ago, a star, much like our Sun, called HD 7977, may have passed as close as Gliese 710 will. Gaia's measurements cannot yet pin down exactly how close. So this is not a rare disaster waiting to happen. It is how life works in a galaxy. The Sun is one star among billions, all of them moving, and every few million years, one of them brushes past. What if the night sky you have always known is not fixed at all, but a slow traffic of stars still on the move? The bigger question is the cloud itself. Some astronomers think the Sun was born in a crowd of sister stars, and that many of the comets in our Oort cloud were once theirs. If they are right, every star that passes is part of a very old exchange. Some of the ice falling in from the dark may have started out around another Sun.

kept_transcript: Look at Orion this winter at the orange star on its shoulder. That star is dying. So is Betelgeuse about to explode and what would you see if it did? It is called Betelgeuse. One day it will blow itself apart and for a few weeks it will shine so brightly that you could see it in the daytime sky. Betelgeuse is a red supergiant. It is enormous. Put it where the sun is and its surface would reach out past the orbit of Mars and out beyond the asteroid belt. It is somewhere between 5 and 700 light years away. Even measuring that is hard because the star is so big and so restless that its center is difficult to pin down. And it is young. Our sun is 4 .5 billion years old and halfway through its life. Betelgeuse is only about 10 million years old and it is already near the end of its life. Why so fast? Because it is heavy. With somewhere around 15 to 20 times the sun's mass it burns its fuel ferociously. It gives out around 100 ,000 times as much light as the sun. Big stars live fast and die young. You can find it yourself. On a winter evening look for the three stars of Orion's belt then go up and to the left. Its surface is cooler than the sun's and that is why it glows orange instead of white. At the end of 2019 something strange happened. Betelgeuse, normally one of the brightest stars in the sky, began to fade. By February 2020 it had dropped to about a third of its usual brightness.
